whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Tableau Next Consultant exam for?

personas.label: Tableau Consultants moving to Next
personas.description: You know classic Tableau consulting and are moving to Tableau Next implementations.

personas.label: Analytics practitioners

personas.label: CRM Analytics / Data 360 consultants

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Next Consultant Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam covers implementing Tableau Next analytics in Salesforce, including a governed semantic model and access controls. Review the platform’s approach alongside familiar Tableau tools.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Exam fee: US$200; retake fee: US$100, plus applicable taxes.
No formal prerequisite: Tableau Consultant or Data Cloud implementation experience is strongly recommended.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice explaining the semantic model, AI-assisted analysis, access controls, and embedding. Compare these with a classic Tableau Desktop or Server setup.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Next Consultant Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the Tableau Next Consultant exam online or at a test center with a proctor. Its questions include multiple-choice and multiple-select formats.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Questions can ask how to model data, use AI-assisted analytics, govern access, or embed Tableau Next content in Salesforce.
bestWayToPass: Review the semantic model: Learn how governed metrics and dimensions can be reused across analytics.
Practice AI-assisted analysis: See how natural-language assistance uses governed definitions to surface insights.
Study access controls: Review row-level security and permissions for analytics content.
Explore embedding: Learn how analytics content can appear in Salesforce pages and external experiences.

expertInsight: Use the official Tableau Next Consultant guide and credential page to set your study scope. Check Tableau Next objectives separately from older Desktop, Server, and classic Consultant materials.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests your ability to implement and maintain scalable Tableau Next analytics solutions on a governed, Data Cloud-native semantic data model, including AI-assisted analytics and embedding. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 65% pass mark.

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Next Consultant: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Semantic Data Model Design
blocks.body: A governed semantic model gives teams shared definitions for metrics and dimensions. Review how Tableau Next uses that model with Data Cloud so analysts can reuse consistent definitions.

blocks.heading: AI-Assisted Analytics
blocks.body: AI-assisted and natural-language exploration depends on the quality of the governed data and metric definitions. Check those definitions when assessing an AI-generated insight.

blocks.heading: Governance and Row-Level Security
blocks.body: Row-level controls determine which data a user can see; content permissions determine which assets they can open. Consider both when designing access to Tableau Next data and content.

blocks.heading: Embedding and Distribution
blocks.body: When embedding analytics in a Salesforce page or another experience, plan how users authenticate and how the source security controls apply. Check performance as well as access.

blocks.heading: Performance and Scalability
blocks.body: Changes to shared calculations and aggregations can affect more than one analysis. Assess performance at the semantic-model level as well as in individual views.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Next Consultant Exam
scenarioTips.intro: In analytics scenarios, look for the requirement that calls for a governed semantic model, then compare the available solutions.

blocks.heading: Default to the semantic model, not a one-off calculation
blocks.body: When several teams need the same metric, consider a governed shared definition before creating separate local calculations.

blocks.heading: Separate data access from content access
blocks.body: Ask whether the problem concerns access to data rows or permission to open an asset; the controls address different needs.

blocks.heading: Question AI-assisted answers that skip governance
blocks.body: Compare an AI-generated result with the governed metric and underlying query. Investigate differences before relying on the result.

blocks.heading: Know when embedding should inherit security
blocks.body: Check that an embedded view applies the intended source access controls for its users.

blocks.heading: Don't assume classic Tableau Server admin knowledge transfers directly
blocks.body: Use classic Tableau experience as background, but verify how Tableau Next handles governance and embedding in its own architecture.

nextCertsAfter.intro: After this credential, round out your Tableau and analytics track:

sampleQuestions.question: Two workbooks show different “Total Revenue” values from the same data. What should the consultant check first?
options: Each workbook may use a local formula instead of the shared metric.
A refresh issue may have left one workbook showing older data from a previous period.
Different font settings may make the revenue values look different on the two dashboards.
The workbooks may have been published on separate days with different data snapshots.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Check whether both workbooks use the shared semantic-model definition for Total Revenue. Local calculations can produce inconsistent values.
whyWrong: A refresh issue can make data stale, but it does not explain different calculation definitions.
Fonts affect appearance, not the calculated revenue value.
Different publish dates may affect freshness, but not the metric definition.

sampleQuestions.question: A sales rep can open a regional dashboard but can see revenue from other regions. What should the consultant review?
options: Review the rep’s row-level security rules.
The dashboard color palette and chart formatting settings.
The workbook title and the naming convention used by the analytics team.
The scheduled refresh time and the frequency of data updates.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Row-level security controls which data rows a user can see.
whyWrong: Color and chart settings do not control access to data rows.
A workbook name does not grant or restrict data access.
Refresh schedules affect how current data is, not which rows a user can see.

sampleQuestions.question: An AI analytics feature returns a number that conflicts with the approved KPI definition. What should the consultant do?
options: Tell the user to trust the AI answer over the approved KPI value.
Disable AI analytics for every user without investigating the mismatch.
Fix the model or query to use the approved KPI definition.
Ignore the difference because it only changes how the chart looks.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Check the governed semantic model or query and correct it so AI-assisted answers follow the approved KPI definition.
whyWrong: The approved KPI definition should remain the source of truth.
Disabling the feature for everyone is premature; first find and fix the underlying issue.
A conflicting KPI can affect decisions, so it is not only a display issue.

sampleQuestions.question: A client embeds a Tableau Next view on a Salesforce record page and asks whether it will show more data than its source dashboard. What should the consultant explain?
options: Embedding automatically expands access to all records in the organization.
The embedded view no longer needs security because Salesforce hosts the page.
Embedded views can only show static images, not live data.
The embedded view should follow the source data’s row-level security.
sampleQuestions.explanation: An embedded view should follow the same governed row-level security as its source.
whyWrong: Embedding should not give the viewer broader access than the source allows.
Security still applies to embedded views.
Tableau Next can show live, governed data in an embedded view.

sampleQuestions.question: A company needs to change the “Net Revenue” formula everywhere. What is the best practice?
options: Update the shared semantic-model definition used by the workbooks.
Edit the formula separately in every workbook that uses the metric.
Rename the metric in one workbook and leave the other workbooks unchanged.
Ask each analyst to remember and re-enter the new formula.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Update the shared semantic-model definition so every workbook that references it uses the same calculation.
whyWrong: Changing every workbook separately can lead to inconsistent formulas.
Renaming one metric does not change the formula in other workbooks.
Relying on memory is difficult to maintain and verify.

sampleQuestions.question: A dashboard became much slower after a complex calculation was added to the semantic model. What should the consultant do first?
options: Buy more licenses for users who open the affected dashboards.
Delete all existing dashboards to reduce the number of views.
Optimize the new calculation and its aggregations.
Change every user’s time zone to improve dashboard performance.
sampleQuestions.explanation: The performance issue followed a new calculation, so review and optimize that calculation and its aggregations first.
whyWrong: More licenses do not address the calculation that caused the slowdown.
Deleting dashboards is not a useful first step in diagnosing the calculation.
Time zone settings do not fix calculation performance.

sampleQuestions.question: A team is moving from Tableau Server to Tableau Next. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Existing workbooks always move over unchanged with no design work.
Tableau Next cannot connect to Data Cloud, so the team must replace it.
Redesign the data model, security, and embedding for Tableau Next.
The only supported migration path is to rebuild every report in Excel.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Migration usually requires adapting data and governance to Tableau Next’s semantic model, as well as reviewing security and embedding.
whyWrong: A direct lift-and-shift may not fit the different architecture and governance model.
Tableau Next is designed to work with Data Cloud.
Migration does not require leaving the analytics platform for Excel.

sampleQuestions.question: Two departments need different default views of the same metric. How can the consultant support them while keeping the metric governed?
options: Give each department a separate data source with no shared definition.
Ask each department to calculate the metric by hand every month.
Force both departments to use one fixed view with no changes.
Create department-specific views or parameters on top of the shared semantic model.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Department-specific views or parameters can vary the presentation while keeping the shared metric definition consistent.
whyWrong: Separate, unrelated data sources can create conflicting definitions.
Manual calculations are hard to maintain and can differ.
One fixed view may not meet both departments’ needs.

sampleQuestions.question: An executive asks which value is the source of truth for a metric used in dashboards and AI queries. What should the consultant point to?
options: The workbook that was created most recently.
The governed semantic-model definition for that metric.
An informal estimate from the executive’s team.
The first matching result from a general web search.
sampleQuestions.explanation: The governed semantic-model definition is the source of truth for the metric across workbooks and AI-assisted queries.
whyWrong: This is the governed definition that shared analytics should use.
An informal estimate is not a governed, verifiable metric.
A public web search is not the organization’s internal metric definition.

sampleQuestions.question: An analyst creates a local field that duplicates a metric from the semantic model. What risk should the consultant explain?
options: The platform will automatically delete the original metric.
The duplicate could drift from the governed metric over time.
The platform will immediately crash when the duplicate field is saved.
The new field will automatically give every user admin access.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A separately maintained duplicate can drift from the governed metric over time.
whyWrong: Creating a duplicate field does not delete the original metric.
This is a consistency risk, not a platform stability issue.
A calculated field does not change user permissions.

sampleQuestions.question: A client asks whether Tableau Next supports natural-language analytics. What is the accurate answer?
options: No. It only supports charts that users build manually.
Yes, with natural-language analytics on the governed model.
Yes, but only people outside the organization can use it.
No. Salesforce removed natural-language features from its analytics products.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Next supports natural-language exploration, and answers use the governed semantic model.
whyWrong: Users can explore with natural language as well as build charts.
The feature is not restricted to external users.
Natural-language analytics is available; it has not been removed from all Salesforce analytics.

sampleQuestions.question: A finance team wants only finance staff to open a workbook. What should the consultant configure?
options: Row-level security only, which filters data after a workbook is opened.
Content or workbook permissions that limit who can open the asset.
A dashboard color change that marks the workbook as internal.
A change to the semantic-model formula for the finance metrics.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Content or workbook permissions control who can open a specific asset.
whyWrong: Row-level security filters which rows an authorized viewer can see; it does not by itself control access to the workbook.
Color does not control access.
Calculation logic changes the metric, not who can open a workbook.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should a consultant avoid copying a governed metric into one workbook as a local calculation?
options: Local calculations are always faster than the semantic model.
A local calculation removes all support for dashboards.
It can drift from the shared metric definition.
It automatically changes the access rights of every user.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A local copy creates another metric definition that can drift from the shared semantic-model definition.
whyWrong: Speed is not guaranteed; the main concern is consistency.
Local calculations do not remove dashboard support.
A local calculation does not change user access.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should an organization use a shared semantic layer instead of letting every team build separate data models?
options: It guarantees that each team will get a different metric value.
It keeps metric definitions consistent and governed across teams.
It removes the need for data governance throughout the organization.
It stops teams from creating their own dashboards.
sampleQuestions.explanation: A shared semantic layer keeps metric definitions consistent and governed across the organization.
whyWrong: Different results across teams are the problem a shared layer helps prevent.
A semantic layer supports governance but does not remove the need for it.
Teams can still create dashboards using shared definitions.

sampleQuestions.question: An Experience Cloud site embeds Tableau Next. An external user should see only data for their account. What should control the data shown?
options: The user’s browser cache and stored page settings.
The site’s page layout template and navigation menu.
The user’s screen size and device type.
Use account-based row-level security.
sampleQuestions.explanation: Row-level security can filter the embedded view to data linked to the logged-in user’s account.
whyWrong: Browser cache does not determine what data the user is authorized to see.
Page layout controls how content is arranged, not which data rows are visible.
Screen size affects display, not access to data.
